5. Operating Procedures

5.1 Installation Positioning
The chip conveyor may be installed at any required position on the machine tool based on user specifications or host machine design requirements. Alternatively, it may be positioned at designated chip removal locations according to workshop layout and machine arrangement. Installation configurations include horizontal, inclined, horizontal-inclined, crossover, or modular combinations. Both fixed positions and support methods are adjustable to accommodate machine tool layouts.
5.2 Placement and Alignment
5.2.1 Position the chip-cooling unit near the host machine.
5.2.2 Adjust the conveyor to align the discharge outlet precisely with the host machine’s coolant inlet.
5.2.3 Level the foundation and adjust anchor bolts to achieve proper height.
Critical tolerance: Foundation leveling error ≤5 mm.
5.3 Piping and Power Connection
5.3.1 Connect pipelines as per provided schematics and position the chip collection tank.
5.3.2 Plug the power connector into the host machine’s designated socket.
5.4 Electrical Wiring
5.4.1 Voltage Compliance: Operate only within the rated voltage range specified for this device.
5.4.2 Grounding Requirement: A functional earth connection must be installed.
5.4.3 Wiring Configuration: Follow the terminal diagram inside the junction box cover. Incorrect wiring may cause motor burnout.
5.4.4 Factory Default Settings:
•    Motors are preconfigured for 3-phase 220V power supply (Delta connection).
•    For 3-phase 380V power supply, reconfigure to Star (Y) connection.
Motor Terminal Configurations:
(Wiring diagrams for Delta and Star connections here.)

IN PUT 3￠AC(△)220V         

IN PUT 3￠AC(Y)380V

5.5 Operation
(Note: The chip conveyor must operate simultaneously with the host machine.)
5.5.1 Pre-Startup Verification
5.5.1.1 Confirm wiring correctness.
5.5.1.2 Inspect terminal blocks for looseness and ensure secure fastening.
5.5.1.3 Validate the integrity of the grounding circuit.
5.5.1.4 Verify that no foreign objects are present on the conveyor chain.
5.5.2 Trial Run Inspection
5.5.2.1 Ensure the conveyor chain rotates in the direction indicated by the arrow markings.
5.5.2.2 Perform a minimum one full cycle of jog operation to detect abnormal vibrations or misalignment.
5.5.3 Normal Operation Guidelines
5.5.3.1 Monitor for abnormal noise, vibration, or overheating during operation.
5.5.3.2 Clear all residual chips from the conveyor chain prior to shutdown.
(Failure to comply may cause overload during restart, leading to jamming or blockage.)
5.5.3.3 Feed chips only after the conveyor reaches full speed. Maintain continuous operation; intermittent use or bulk chip loading is prohibited.
5.5.3.4 Inspect chain tension, parallelism, and wear condition periodically.
5.5.3.5 For wet machining (coolant tank with pump operation):
Strictly prohibit dry running to prevent pump seal damage.
5.5.3.6 Prevent tools or workpieces from falling into the conveyor during operation.
5.5.3.7 Do not open protective covers or insert body parts/foreign objects into access points during operation.
(Critical safety measure to avoid injuries.)
5.5.3.8 In case of power failure, disconnect the power supply to prevent unintended restart hazards.

The reverse rotation function is strictly reserved for maintenance purposes. Activating reverse mode during normal operation will void warranties and may cause mechanical failure or personal injury. All liabilities arising from improper use shall be borne by the operator.

6. Maintenance

6.1 Lubrication
6.1.1 The reducer motor is factory-sealed with lubricant and requires no additional greasing.
6.1.2 For dry operation (no coolant), periodically lubricate the conveyor chain.
6.1.3 Lubricate the drive chain at regular intervals. Ensure friction plates remain clean and free of oil contamination.
(Oil on friction plates compromises torque protection performance.)

6.2 Chain Tension Adjustment
(Long-term use may reduce chain tension. Adjust as follows:)
6.2.1 Loosen the fixing nuts on the reducer motor mounting plate and lower it slightly to slacken the drive chain.
6.2.2 Adjust the tensioning bolts on the conveyor chain to achieve proper tension. Ensure equal bolt protrusion on both sides, then tighten the locknuts.
6.2.3 Raise the reducer motor mounting plate to restore drive chain tension and secure all nuts.

If no adjustment range remains after prolonged use, remove two chain plates before reassembly to restore proper tension.

6.3 Conveyor Internal Cleaning
Perform full internal cleaning annually. Follow these steps for chain removal and reinstallation:
6.3.1 Locate the chain connection point and position it at the discharge opening (cotter pin location).
6.3.2 Fully release the tensioning bolts.
6.3.3 Use dedicated tools to remove retaining pins, ball bearings, and side plates.
6.3.4 Extract the conveyor chain from the top (pull out the upper chain layer).
6.3.5 Remove accumulated chips from the conveyor interior.
6.3.6 Reassemble in reverse order, ensuring scraper plates (side plates) are oriented correctly.

7. Troubleshooting and Solutions

7.1 Conveyor Failure to Operate
7.1.1 Motor Inoperability
Initial verification steps:
7.1.1.1 Confirm power supply voltage matches specifications.
7.1.1.2 Verify proper grounding connection.
7.1.1.3 Check wiring configuration against the terminal diagram in the junction box.
(Mismatched voltage/wiring may cause motor burnout. Refer to Section 5.4.4 for factory settings: 3-phase 220V Delta connection or 3-phase 380V Star (Y) connection.)
If wiring is correct but motor remains inoperative:
Cause: Thermal overload relay tripped due to excessive load.
Solution:
De-energize the system.
Clear overloaded chips from the conveyor.
Reset the thermal overload relay.
Restart and operate the conveyor unloaded for 3–5 minutes to verify normal function.
7.1.2 Chain Plate/Chain Failure to Rotate
Causes:
① Chain plate/chains jammed due to overload; ② Torque limiter slippage.

Solutions:
① For overload conditions:
Immediately de-energize the system.
Clear overloaded chips.
(Note: Chain plate conveyors are suitable for long chips, but chip length must not exceed 300–500 mm. Excessive lengths may cause plate jamming. For unavoidable long chips, modify CNC programs to shorten chips or use dual-layer chain plate conveyors. Scraper-type conveyors strictly prohibit long coiled chips to avoid entanglement and jamming.)
② For torque limiter slippage:
Recalibrate the torque limiter to the factory preset value of 90 N·m.
7.2 Chips Accumulating in Conveyor Base
Cause:
Chips adhere to chains at the discharge outlet and re-enter the conveyor, accumulating at the base.
Solutions:
① Activate reverse operation mode to expel accumulated chips via backward chain movement.
② Place cotton rags on the chain surface, run the conveyor in reverse 2–3 times to mechanically remove residual chips.
7.3 Chain Side Plate Disengagement
Cause:
Abrasion between chain plates, guides, or chips during operation leads to plate wear and side plate detachment.
Solution: Replace worn chain plates.
Procedure:
① Clear chips and operate the conveyor unloaded until the damaged section aligns with the discharge opening.
② Remove the worn chain plate using an angle grinder.
③ Install a new chain plate.
7.4 Chain Plate Fracture
Causes:
① Large workpieces/tools falling into the conveyor; ② Overload operation (torque limiter fails to slip despite motor functioning).
Solutions:
① Clear debris and operate unloaded to position the fractured plate at the discharge opening. Replace the damaged plate.
② Adjust the torque limiter with a calibrated torque wrench to ensure slippage under overload, preventing chain plate rupture.

8. Consumables

Motor drive sprocket, drive chain, torque limiter, chain plate sprocket, chain plate assembly, scraper plates, scraper chain, bearings, proximity sensor, steel wire brush, filter cartridge.
When ordering consumables, provide:
Equipment model
Component name
Unit serial number

9. Warranty

The product is warranted against defects in materials and workmanship for one (1) year from the date of purchase. To claim warranty service:
Submit a completed Quality Feedback Form and original purchase invoice to our sales department.
Our technicians will diagnose the fault.
Repairs/replacements will be provided at no charge if the defect is confirmed as manufacturing-related.
Warranty Exclusions:
① Damage caused by unauthorized repairs or part replacements.
② Failures due to:Improper installation/Incorrect voltage input
/Operator error/Force majeure (e.g., accidents, natural disasters).

10. Appendix
10.1 Component Replacement Guidelines
Chain plates, scrapers, and chains require periodic replacement. Service life varies with chip morphology, operating conditions, and runtime. Monitor wear during routine inspections.

10.2 Conveyor Selection Guidance
To optimize chip removal efficiency, conveyor selection should align with the machining process and chip characteristics:

For turning or drilling operations generating coiled, clustered, or long continuous chips (≥50 mm), prioritize chain plate conveyors or dual-layer chain plate systems, which excel in handling extended swarf without jamming.

For milling, planing, or drilling producing discontinuous, flaky, or powdery chips, employ scraper conveyors, magnetic scrapers, screw conveyors, or hybrid configurations to manage fragmented or fine debris effectively.

Exclusive iron chip processing demands high-strength magnetic conveyors for reliable ferrous material extraction.

Lightweight metallic/non-metallic powders, such as aluminum or plastic residues, are best handled by reverse-flow drum-type conveyors, which prevent dust dispersion through controlled centrifugal separation.

2.1    Fundamental Safety Precautions

Thoroughly read the machine manual and safety labels affixed to the machine

▲    Before installing, operating, maintaining, servicing, or repairing the machine, carefully study this manual to fully understand its contents, operational methods, and potential causes of personal injury or machine damage.

▲    Safety labels on the machine indicate areas of potential hazards. Read and comprehend these warnings thoroughly.

Machine Application Scope

▲    This machine is a CNC horizontal lathe designed for metal cutting. Do not use it for purposes outside its original design specifications.

▲    Perform machining only within the machine’s rated working range.

▲    Use the fixtures provided with the machine whenever possible. If alternative fixtures or tooling equipment are selected, ensure the spindle speed does not exceed the fixture/tooling’s maximum allowable speed. Verify proper workpiece clamping before operation. Our company shall not be liable for injuries or equipment damage

Follow all workshop regulations and operate the machine safely

▲    Operation is typically performed by a single operator. If multiple operators are required, clarify roles, sequences, and actions in advance, and execute under unified command.

▲    Do not operate the machine under fatigue, illness, emotional distress, or under the influence of alcohol/medication. Impaired judgment may lead to malfunctions, injuries, or equipment damage.

Wear Appropriate Safety Gear

▲    Operators must wear dedicated workwear, safety shoes, caps, and safety goggles to ensure personal protection.

▲    Avoid gloves, loose ties, scarves, or dangling accessories during operation to prevent entanglement in moving/rotating parts, which may cause severe injuries.

Maintain a Safe Workspace

▲    Keep the machine area clean and free of clutter. Immediately clean spills of lubricants or coolants to avoid slip hazards.

▲    Ensure sufficient clearance around the machine.

▲    Do not place tools, parts, or objects on machine guards, doors, slides, or other areas that may interfere with operation.

Fire Prevention

▲    Lubricants and coolants used in the machine are flammable. Handle with extreme caution.

▲    Ensure fire prevention and extinguishing equipment is available near the machine.

▲    Keep flammable materials and high-temperature devices away from the machine.

Unauthorized Modifications Prohibited

▲    Structural modifications to the machine are strictly prohibited without prior written approval from our company.

▲    We shall not be held liable for injuries or damage caused by unauthorized alterations or usage beyond permitted specifications.

Electrical and Maintenance Safety

▲    Ensure the machine’s electrical system is grounded in compliance with the GB5226.1-2002 standard before operation. Do not touch controllers or switches with wet hands. High-voltage components (e.g., electrical cabinets, transformers, motors) must only be inspected or repaired by qualified personnel.

▲    Avoid connecting power cables from interference-generating devices (e.g., welding machines, high-frequency hardening equipment) to the control panel

▲    Clearly label the machine as “FAULTY — DO NOT USE” during repair.

▲    All maintenance must be performed by certified technicians after disconnecting the power supply and switching the main breaker to [OFF].

2.2    Operational Precautions

Pre-Use Precautions for Initial Operation

▲    While the machine is equipped with multiple safety devices to protect operators and equipment, do NOT rely solely on these safeguards. Strictly adhere to operational safety protocols to prevent hazards caused by device malfunctions or failures. Thoroughly review this manual and ensure operators are professionally trained and certified before use.

▲    Remove all transportation locks on protective doors before operation. Failure to do so may damage the machine.

▲    Prior to initial operation, thoroughly remove all preservative oil from the machine surfaces using kerosene and lubricate all designated lubrication points in accordance with the manufacturer's specifications.

▲    Do NOT use deteriorated or contaminated lubricants.

Safety Device Verification

▲    Verify proper functionality of all safety devices before operation.  Do NOT operate the machine until repairs are completed if any device is faulty:

▲    Check the accuracy of X/Z-axis soft limits and mechanical limit switches before machining.

▲    Confirm the emergency stop button is responsive and reliable.

Operational Guidelines

▲    Gloves are prohibited during operation.

▲    Do NOT open doors during machine operation.

▲    Do NOT touch moving parts with hands or tools.

▲    For long bar stock extending beyond the spindle, install warning signs or protective barriers to prevent injuries.

▲    Immediately stop the machine and perform maintenance if abnormal noise or vibration occurs. Resume operation only after troubleshooting.

▲    Memorize the location of the emergency stop button to enable instant activation during emergencies.

▲    Remove chips promptly. 

▲    Always power off the machine before cleaning the machining area. Use dedicated cleaning tools to remove chips.  DO NOT handle chips with bare hands—they are high-temperature and sharp-edged, posing severe injury risks.

▲    Implement strict protocols for machine organization, routine maintenance, and workspace cleanliness to ensure optimal performance and longevity.

▲    CNC (Computer Numerical Control) and PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) parameters are factory-preset and typically require no adjustments.

▲    If modifications are necessary: Fully understand the functional implications of each parameter. Perform changes ONLY under the supervision of our certified technicians.

▲    DO NOT alter technical parameters beyond the machine’s rated specifications, including: Maximum spindle speed, Rapid traverse rates of tool posts and Other critical thresholds.

▲    Our company shall not be held liable for equipment damage, injuries, or accidents resulting from unauthorized modifications.

2.3    Waste Disposal

▲    Waste lubricants and cutting fluids generated during replacement must not be directly discharged onto the ground or into drainage systems. All waste liquids must be properly stored or disposed of at designated locations specified by environmental protection authorities.

▲    For non-recyclable toxic, hazardous, or non-degradable waste (e.g., electrical components, rubber parts, lubricants) generated during final machine scrapping, disposal must comply with relevant regulations.

3.1    Main Structure

The L2 Series CNC Lathe adopts a flat guideway saddle structure, with the X-axis carriage featuring a 30° inclined configuration. Capable of optional hydraulic tailstock integration, it represents the standard configuration universally adopted in modern entry-level and full-function CNC lathes. The machine delivers high rigidity, exceptional machining flexibility, robust chip protection, efficient chip evacuation, and user-friendly operation. Its modular structural design and fully enclosed guarding ensure operational reliability. 

3.2    Key Characteristics

3.2.1 The bed is cast from premium HT300 gray cast iron in an integral box-type structure, optimized through finite element analysis and reinforced with strategically distributed ribs. This design delivers exceptional rigidity and thermal stability.  The right or rear chip removal configuration provides large chip capacity and enhances flexibility for workshop layout optimization and space utilization.

3.2.2 Equipped with a flat guideway bed and a 30° inclined X-axis carriage, this compact structure delivers superior rigidity and excellent thermal stability.

3.2.3 The L2/L2L models adopt a box-type high-rigidity triple-disc servo turret, providing rapid tool change and excellent chip resistance. The L2LD model utilizes a Taiwan BMT45 or German Schaudt VDI30 12-station power turret, which can be flexibly configured with either power tool holders or fixed tool holders. The power tool holders are equipped with high-performance servo motors capable of reaching rotational speeds up to 4,000 rpm, enabling them to effortlessly handle machining processes such as turning, milling, drilling, and tapping of components.

3.2.4 The guideways employ high-quality linear roller guides from Taiwan, which significantly improve rigidity and service life. Featuring high-speed movement, superior precision retention, and ease of maintenance, these guideways are specifically designed for precision machining applications.

3.2.5 Imported precision ball screws are used on both axes, providing fast, stable, and highly accurate movement. Each screw adopts a pre-tensioned, double-supported structure with dedicated bearings. The pre-tensioning, precisely calculated and assembled, effectively minimizes machining accuracy deviations caused by thermal expansion of the screws.

3.2.6 The spindle assembly adopts a high-rigidity A2-6 spindle unit, with a maximum spindle speed of 4,000 rpm. The high-rigidity symmetrical spindle box is equipped with an 8-inch hydraulic chuck, ensuring high spindle stiffness and minimal thermal deformation.

3.2.7 The main motor is standardly configured with an 11 kW high-performance spindle servo motor, delivering high spindle output torque, high rotational speed, and a wide speed regulation range.

3.2.8 This series offers two models for selection: one with a hydraulic tailstock and one without. The tailstock sleeve taper hole can accommodate a Morse No. 4 center, while the tailless model provides more unobstructed chip evacuation space.

3.2.9 The machine features two lubrication methods: grease lubrication and oil lubrication. Spindle bearings and screw bearings use long-life grease lubrication for extended service and maintenance-free operation. Screw pairs and guideways are lubricated by an automatic centralized oil system, ensuring reliable and adequate lubrication.

3.2.10 Equipped with LED lighting—energy-efficient, high-performance, and long-lasting. Features a three-color status indicator for real-time machine operation monitoring, enabling intuitive visual management on the shop floor.

3.2.11· This machine features a compact design, sleek appearance, and fully enclosed guards for reliable protection, along with efficient chip evacuation. It is equipped with high-strength tempered safety glass windows, bright work lighting, and an ergonomic operating height for optimal comfort.

The following usage and machining methods are prohibited, as they may cause personal injury or machine tool failure.

Always refer to the Machine Tool Safety Guidelines for safe operation practices.

•    Operate within the permissible rotational speed range of the spindle, chuck, and hydraulic cylinder.

•    Failure to comply may result in workpiece ejection, leading to personal injury or machine damage. 

•    Always close the front door during operation.

•    Do not operate with covers removed or movable parts exposed.

•    Violation may cause entanglement in rotating parts or pinching by moving components, resulting in severe injury.

•    Never operate the machine after removing or modifying safety devices, protective covers, or safety windows.

•    Violation may cause entanglement in rotating parts or pinching by moving components, resulting in severe injury.

•    Do not operate the machine when bar stock protrudes from the rear of the spindle.

•    Rotating extended bar stock may vibrate excessively, causing injury or machine damage.

Never mount cutting tools on the spindle side for machining.

Example:
Prohibited: Installing workpieces on the turret and tools on the spindle for milling operations.
Violation may cause machine damage.

During workpiece clamping with the chuck:

•    Do not feed the turret in Z/X-axis directions while the spindle is stationary for keyway machining or planning operations.

•    Such operations generate abnormal thrust on feed-system ball screws, potentially causing mechanical failure.

•    Avoid using compressed air to remove chips inside the machine.

•    Scattered chips may infiltrate unintended areas of the inclined structure, leading to machine malfunctions.

When machining flammable materials or substances generating hazardous byproducts:

•    Consult specialists and implement protective gear, safety devices, or environmental controls.

•    Negligence may result in fire accidents or chemical exposure injuries.

•    Operators must receive proper NC lathe operation training and guidance.

•    Failure to comply may cause injury during maintenance or machine damage.

•    Maintenance personnel must undergo NC lathe operation/maintenance training.

•    Qualified electricians or crane operators should be employed as needed.

Article body:
Before initiating machining, ensure the following elements are confirmed:

1)    Workpiece clamping method

2)    Suitable tools meeting process requirements

3)    Proper cutting parameters and CNC program aligned with process specifications

The operating procedures for the L2 series, including optional functions, are described below:

4.1    Workpiece Clamping Methods

4.1.1 The workpiece clamping method of this machine tool generally utilizes a hollow hydraulic chuck.

4.1.2 The spindle is standardly equipped with an 8-inch hydraulic chuck. 

4.1.3 During assembly, ensure the draw tube is fully threaded into the hydraulic cylinder and chuck. Improper connections may cause machine damage.

4.1.4 The total system pressure of the hydraulic power unit can be adjusted via the regulating screw on the hydraulic pump, typically set to 40 kgf/cm². Hydraulic cylinder operation
The cylinder operates using hydraulic pressure, which can be adjusted by rotating the regulating knob of the pressure-reducing valve. The maximum allowable working pressure for the 8-inch hollow power chuck must not exceed 26 kgf.

4.1.5 The through-hole chuck design enables bar stock feeding for continuous machining.

4.1.6 For long bar stock processing, integrate with a bar feeder.

4.1.7 Optional clamping solutions include solid hydraulic chucks, pneumatic chucks, collet chucks, or custom fixtures. Unauthorized fixture modifications are prohibited. Damage or safety incidents caused by such actions are not covered by the manufacturer’s liability.

4.2    Workpiece Support Methods

4.2.1 For CNC machine tools without hydraulic tailstock functionality, the workpiece support method is as follows.

The spindle chuck clamps one end of the workpiece and rotates it, while the cutting tool mounted on the turret performs machining operations. The recommended maximum length-to-diameter ratio is 1:5.

Long Bar Processing Integrate with a long bar feeder for continuous machining of extended workpieces.

4.2.2 For CNC machine tools equipped with a single chuck and hydraulic tailstock function, the workpiece support method is as follows:

a) Chuck-Tailstock Support (One-Clamp-One-Center)

Clamp one end of the workpiece with the left mechanical spindle chuck and support the opposite end with the tailstock center. The workpiece rotates for turret-based cutting.

b) Dual Tailstock Support (Two-Center Method)

Mount a center on the left spindle end and support both workpiece ends with tailstock centers. The workpiece rotates for cutting. Critical Notes: Insecure workpiece fixation may cause tool damage or machine failure. Ensure the spindle labyrinth seal remains effective to prevent coolant ingress and machine damage.

4.3    Workpiece Loading/Unloading Techniques

Workpiece handling includes manual and automated methods.

4.3.1 Manual Operation

Directly load/unload workpieces into/from the chuck by hand.

4.3.2 Gantry/Articulated Robot Handling

A method in which a gantry robot or articulated robot automatically picks up unfinished parts from the material tray and loads them into the chuck for machining, or unloads finished parts from the chuck and places them into the tray.

This method enables continuous automation, improves efficiency, reduces labor, and supports high-volume production.

4.3.3 Bar Feeder Method

Automatically feed bar stock through the spindle draw tube bore from the machine’s left side.
Repeatedly perform cutting, machining, and feeding of bar stock in sequence.

4.3.4 Workpiece Catcher Method

Collect finished parts cut from continuous bar machining and eject them outside the machine.
Typical Application: Combined with a bar feeder on the supply side for seamless production.

4.4    Chip Handling Methods

To discharge chips from the machine or remove chips near the workpiece and cutting tool, the following methods are available:

4.4.1 Manual Chip Disposal

A manual chip collection box is installed within the machine bed cavity. During chip removal, manually scrape chips out of the machine using tools.

4.4.2 Chip Conveyor System

An optional chain-type automatic chip conveyor can be installed in the machine bed cavity. The conveyor supports two discharge orientations: right-side discharge or rear discharge. During machining, chips falling into the conveyor are automatically expelled from the machine into a chip collection trolley positioned below the conveyor outlet.

4.4.3 Chip Removal at Machining Zone

Chip removal and tooltip cooling are typically achieved via coolant spray nozzles mounted on the tool turret. In specific cases, high-pressure air blast may be employed.

4.4.4 High-Pressure Chip Flushing

For materials prone to continuous chips or deep-hole machining, an optional high-pressure cutting oil pump can be installed to flush chips using pressurized cutting oil.

4.5    Cutting Fluid Application Guidelines

During cutting operations, tool temperature rises significantly due to high-intensity pressure processing. To mitigate cutting resistance, suppress built-up edge (BUE) formation, cool the tool, improve surface finish on precision-machined workpieces, enhance dimensional accuracy, prolong tool life, and facilitate chip evacuation, the use of appropriate cutting fluids is critical. 

4.5.1 Cutting Fluid Delivery

The machine is equipped with an independent coolant tank beneath the bed. A coolant pump delivers cutting fluid from the tank to the machining zone through turret-mounted nozzles for cooling and chip flushing.

4.5.2 Cutting Fluid Storage

The cutting fluid is stored in an independent coolant tank located beneath the machine bed, with a capacity of approximately 90 liters.
Maintaining adequate fluid levels prevents machine thermal expansion and ensures stable machining accuracy.

4.5.3 Cutting Fluid Selection

Select fluids based on workpiece material and machining requirements. Improper selection may degrade tool life and part accuracy.

4.5.4 The coolant tank filter must be cleaned frequently to ensure that cutting fluid flows adequately and smoothly through the coolant lines. 

4.5.6 When connecting the main power supply to the machine, the coolant pump must be removed and lifted out of the coolant tank. Activate the coolant pump and verify that the impeller rotation direction aligns with the arrow indicator on the pump housing. If the rotation direction is incorrect, reverse the phase sequence of the power supply and retest until proper rotation is confirmed.  Failure to correct the rotation direction will result in reduced coolant flow and premature pump failure.

4.6    Optional Accessories

4.6.1 Automatic Tool Setter

The machine can be equipped with a precision automatic tool-setting system. This device automatically detects tool tip positions under program control, enabling rapid generation of the initial machining position in the control system. Additionally, periodic re-detection of tool tip positions compensates for tool wear, ensuring consistent machining accuracy during prolonged operations.

4.6.2 Bar Feeder

For installation and operation of the bar feeder, refer to the electrical circuit diagrams provided with the machine and the bar feeder’s dedicated user manual.

4.6.3 Pneumatic Automatic Part Catcher

The machine may be optionally configured with a pneumatic part-catching system. The sequence is as follows:

1）After completing all machining operations on a workpiece held by the chuck, the system program activates a cylinder-driven mechanism. This rotates the collection box clockwise to position it beneath the workpiece. The cutoff tool on the turret severs the finished part, which then falls into the collection box.

2) Under CNC program control, the pneumatic cylinder rotates the collection box counterclockwise to tilt the workpiece onto a conveyor belt. The belt, driven by a gear motor, transports the workpiece from the right side of the machine into a secondary collection bin. Once multiple parts have accumulated in the bin, an operator can manually retrieve them.

4.6.4 In-Process Workpiece Inspection System

The machine can be optionally equipped with an in-process workpiece inspection system. The wireless inspection receiver is mounted above the spindle, and the contact-type probe is installed on the turret’s boring tool holder. After the workpiece machining is completed, the turret can be program-controlled to move the probe into contact with the workpiece. The system detects deviation values of the workpiece and automatically compensates for them in the CNC program, ensuring machining accuracy.

4.6.5 High-Pressure Coolant Pump System

The high-pressure coolant pump system can be selected based on application requirements. It is designed for chip-breaking and tool tip cooling during part machining, effectively prolonging tool life while ensuring optimal compatibility with automated loading/unloading mechanisms.

2.5    Cutting Fluids 

Cutting fluids are classified into two types: non-water-soluble cutting fluids and water-soluble cutting fluids. 

These fluids possess primary properties related to cutting performance, tool life, and machining surface accuracy, as well as secondary properties related to factors like corrosion resistance, safety, and cost-effectiveness, which make them easier to use.

Improper use of cutting fluids can lead to machine tool malfunctions. Please consider the following factors when selecting a cutting fluid:

(1) Primary Properties (Performance that Enhances Cutting Efficiency)

•    Reduces cutting resistance, eliminates built-up edge, and improves machining surface accuracy.

•    Lowers cutting temperature and extends tool life.

(2) Secondary Properties (User-Friendly Features) 

•    Prevents rust on both the workpiece and the machined part. 

•    Produces minimal smoke and mist.

•    Consistent quality (no separation or layering, with non-aging properties). 

•    Non-harmful to human health (including no unpleasant odors).

•    Does not affect coatings.

The user is responsible for preparing the cutting fluid. When adding fluid, monitor the oil level in the tank, typically filling it to about 3/4 of the tank's height.

2)    Confirm the installation of the turning tools and boring bars. 

3)    Verify the condition of the cutting edges and wear of the turning tools and boring bars. 

4)    Confirm the installation of the chuck jaws. 

5)    Check for any damage to the dust scraper or sliding protective covers.

7.1    Classification of Machine Lubricants

The lubrication of this machine tool is divided into grease lubrication and oil lubrication.

7.1.1 Grease Lubrication

The bearings of this machine tool are lubricated with high-speed long-life grease, requiring no maintenance under normal operating conditions.

7.1.2 Oil Lubrication

The lubrication of linear guides, ball screw nuts, and transmission gears in the power tool turret is achieved through a centralized oil supply from an automatic lubrication pump. The system will trigger an alarm when the oil level in the pump’s reservoir is insufficient. Immediately refill the reservoir upon such an alarm.

7.1.3 Recommended lubricating oil: ISO32 mineral-based lubricating oil. Users can adjust the lubrication cycle according to demand. 

To ensure sufficient lubrication at all points, the manufacturer recommends setting the lubrication pump to operate every 30 minutes, with each cycle lasting no less than 10 seconds. If improper settings result in insufficient lubrication and cause machine damage, the company assumes no liability.

7.1.4 Precautions 

•    All lubricants must be clean and free from contamination. 
•    Regularly inspect the lubrication pump and replenish oil promptly. Replace contaminated oil immediately.

7.3    Lubrication Unit 

The lubrication unit adopts a resistance-type electric oil pump. 

Lubrication intervals are adjustable.

Equipped with a liquid level sensor: a buzzer will alarm and send an error signal to the control system when oil is low.

Article body:
This chapter provides instructions in the sequence from machine installation to operation.

•    During collaborative work, ensure mutual coordination and verification.

•    Thoroughly read and understand the [Safety Guidelines] before operation.

•    Install protective barriers and warning signs (e.g., "No Entry") in the work area.

•    Operators must wear safety helmets, safety shoes, and appropriate work attire.

Subcategory: Section C Machine Tool Transportation and Installation

Article body:
•    Install the machine tool under appropriate environmental conditions.

•    Failure to comply may lead to malfunctions in the main unit or peripheral electrical systems, resulting in machine failure.

1.1    Installation Environment

NC lathes are equipped with precision components. To maximize performance and extend service life, proper environmental conditions must be maintained.

The machine must be installed indoors, protected from weather, with careful attention to ambient temperature, dust, vibration, and noise levels.

Environmental Conditions

•    Ambient Temperature: 0–35°C
•    Temperature Fluctuation: ≤1.1°C/min
•    Humidity: ≤75% (at 20°C)
•    Optimal Surrounding Temperature: 17–26°C
•    Daily Temperature Variation: Within ±2° Cover 24 hours
•    Vibration: ≤0.5 G

Notes on Environmental Setup

1)    Do not install the machine outdoors. 
Avoid direct sunlight or HVAC airflow.
Significant temperature variations will directly affect machining accuracy.

2)    Avoid locations with excessive vibration or noise from nearby equipment. machine failure and adversely impact machining precision.

3)    Avoid humid (≥76%), dusty, or foggy environments. This may lead to machine failure.

4)    Do not place unrelated items near the machine.

1.2    Foundation

To ensure optimal machining precision, the machine must be installed on a firm and stable foundation. 
Depending on the ground conditions at the installation site, the foundation should be constructed using standard methods for machine tool installation. (Refer to: Foundation Drawing)

Notes on Foundation Work

1)    Typically, the concrete thickness of the factory floor should be 300 mm.
2)    The bearing capacity must be ≥ 0.05 MPa.
3)    The foundation should extend approximately 300 mm beyond the machine base.
4)    When selecting the installation location, consider: Access for opening/closing the control cabinet；Space for the chip conveyor；Space for the cutting oil tank；and Maintenance clearance.

1)    Use a precision level with sensitivity of 0.02 mm/m to check the horizontal level. Place it on the base slide surface and check along both Z-axis and X-axis directions. 

2)    Adjust the leveling screws at the lower part of the base until the bubble in the level is centered.

Article body:
To minimize the impact of heat generated during the initial automatic operation on workpiece machining accuracy, preheating of the spindle and all moving axes should be performed before automatic operation. 

When preparing the preheating program, in addition to spindle operation (1000 rpm) and rapid feed movements, please include a program that covers various functions. 

•    Caution If the machine has been idle for an extended period (over one week), suddenly running the spindle at high speeds could damage the spindle's oil film, leading to bearing wear.

In such cases, set the spindle speed to 300 rpm for about 30 minutes, then increase to 500 rpm for another 30 minutes for preheating. For detailed information about preheating operations, please contact the manufacturer.

•    During Automatic Operation Warning

•    If any inspection results are unsatisfactory, immediately stop the machine tool.

•    Do not operate the machine until repairs or fixes have been completed. 

•    Failure to comply may cause injury during maintenance or machine damage.

1)    Confirm the operational sound and vibration of the spindle during operation. 

2)    Confirm the sound of the spindle motor during operation.   

3)    Confirm the vibration during automatic operation. 

4)    Confirm the load status of the spindle motor (data can be monitored on the system display screen).

5)    Confirm the machining accuracy of the workpiece.

•    Do not use compressed air to clean the inside of the machine tool. 

•    Flying chips may enter unintended areas such as guideways, which can lead to machine malfunctions.  

Use a brush and cloth to clean the interior of the machine tool. 

Remove chips from the base and chip conveyor, disposing of them outside the machine, and transport.

chips from the chip cart to the designated disposal area.

Personnel Maintenance work involves various risks, and personnel must be attentive and careful while performing maintenance tasks.

Maintenance personnel should observe the following precautions: 

•    When working with electrical systems, always disconnect the power supply and lock the main switch. 

•    Failure to do so can lead to electric shocks, entanglement in rotating parts, or being caught in moving components. 

•    Always display a "Do Not Energize" warning during maintenance tasks. 

•    -Electrical system maintenance should only be carried out by personnel designated as responsible for maintenance by the factory. 

•    Performing electrical work without proper electrical safety knowledge can lead to electrocution risks. 

•    When working together, always confirm with others before proceeding with operations. 

•    Failure to confirm can result in electric shocks, entanglement in rotating parts, or being caught in moving components.   

•   When entering the machine for maintenance or inspection, always disconnect the power supply.

•    Performing maintenance or inspections with the power on increases the risk of unintended machine movements, which could lead to entanglement in rotating parts or injury from moving components.

•    Always wear protective equipment and appropriate work attire suited for the job. 

•    Failure to do so can lead to personal injuries such as cuts, bumps, and entanglement in rotating parts. 

•    During maintenance, ensure that a "Maintenance Work in Progress" sign is posted to inform others that maintenance is taking place. 

•    Failure to do so may result in accidental machine operation by personnel unaware of the ongoing maintenance, potentially causing injury. 

•    Use the proper tools for the maintenance tasks at hand. 

•    Using inappropriate tools can lead to personal injuries and machine damage. 

•    When handling heavy objects, use a crane. 

•    Failure to do so may result in losing balance and injury from falling objects. 

•    Never use frayed or knotted ropes.  Using damaged ropes can result in the object being dropped, leading to potential injury.

6.1    Hydraulic Chuck Maintenance

6.1.1 Regular disassembly and cleaning of the chuck is required. During reassembly, apply oil as needed. 

6.1.2 Inspection Items and Cycle for Chuck Maintenance: 

•    Disassembly and cleaning: Every 1000 hours 

•    Clamping accuracy check: Every 500 hours 

•    Stroke check: Every 500 hours 

•    Chuck jaw cleaning: Every 8 hours  

•    Main jaw lubrication: Every 8 hours   

6.1.3 Grease the chuck using a grease gun (if there is insufficient grease in the main jaw, clamping force will decrease). 

Recommended grease: Molybdenum disulfide grease.

Lubrication Method

For lubrication procedures, refer to [Chapter D, 2.4 Lubricants]. 

When adding coolant to the chuck, ensure that the frequency of lubrication is increased, and always check that the grease is not exhausted. 

6.2    Hydraulic Cylinder Maintenance 

6.2.1 If oil leakage occurs, disassemble, clean, and replace the O-ring. 

6.2.2 During reassembly, ensure that the hydraulic piping is connected correctly. 

6.2.3 Inspection Items and Cycle:  

Cutting oil recovery port: Every 8 hours

This section outlines the key points for regular maintenance and adjustments to maintain the machine tool's accuracy and longevity. 

Maintenance personnel should also refer to other manuals for specific maintenance procedures.

The primary objective of maintenance inspections is to detect any abnormalities in the machine early, preventing potential failures, thereby increasing machine uptime and productivity. 

To achieve this, it is essential to create a maintenance schedule based on the [Regular Inspection Checklist], and for maintenance personnel to perform inspections and maintenance according to the schedule. 

Additionally, it is important to consider feedback from daily inspectors and make any necessary adjustments. 

Besides this manual, maintenance should also refer to the operation manuals, electrical diagrams, and ladder diagrams.

To conduct maintenance effectively, ensure the following preparations are made.

By properly preparing, even emergency repairs can be completed quickly. 

Consult with the operator responsible for the machine to understand any abnormal conditions.  

Investigate the situation, plan the scope of work, and establish the sequence of tasks. 

Familiarize yourself with the specifications, structure, and functionality of the maintenance points in advance. 

If working with other departments, ensure thorough discussions and coordination beforehand.   

If parts or consumables need to be replaced, make sure to have them prepared in advance.   
Prepare necessary tools, ladders, and step stools for the work.

Please perform inspections and maintenance according to the upcoming scheduled maintenance details, and cross-check with the daily inspection items.

Because belt tension affects both cutting efficiency and service life, setting the correct tension is extremely important.

Over time, belts can lose tension due to elongation and wear from continuous operation, requiring regular inspection and adjustment.

To adjust the belt tension, loosen the four fixed screws on the motor base and use the adjustment bolts to modify the tension.

Article title: Understanding Life Cycle Stages in HubSpot
Article subtitle: In this video, I explain the life cycle stages in HubSpot, focusing on the distinctions between leads and opportunities.
Article body:
In this video, I explain the life cycle stages in HubSpot, focusing on the distinctions between leads and opportunities. A lead is an interested but unqualified contact, while an opportunity indicates a qualified sales engagement with clear intent to purchase. I walk you through the process of moving a contact from the lead stage to the opportunity stage and highlight the importance of qualification. I recommend keeping the sales cycle to 3 to 4 months, and I encourage you to engage with leads effectively to convert them into opportunities. Please make sure to follow the outlined steps to ensure successful deal tracking and conversion.

Understanding Life Cycle Stages in HubSpot

 

1. Introduction to Life Cycle Stages 0:00

  • Explanation of life cycle stages in HubSpot.

  • Focus on key stages: Lead, Opportunity, Customer, Ambassador, Partner.

 

2. Defining Lead and Opportunity 0:28

  • Lead:

    • Represents an interested but unqualified contact.

    • Example: A person who visited the website and checked prices but hasn't been contacted.

  • Opportunity:

    • A qualified sales engagement with clear intent to purchase.

    • Distinction: Qualification and intent are key.

 

3. Moving from Lead to Opportunity 2:03

  • Process of qualifying a lead:

    • Start by reaching out to the lead.

    • Track engagement status: New, Attempting to Connect, Connected, Qualified, Disqualified.

    • If qualified, move the lead to opportunity.

 

4. Creating a Deal 3:50

  • Upon qualification, a deal is created automatically.

  • Example of deal creation:

    • Name the deal (e.g., New Dealer).

    • Assign to the sales pipeline.

 

5. Tracking the Deal Progress 5:56

  • Overview of deal stages:

    • Discuss machine requirements.

    • Send quotes and negotiate.

    • Duration of the deal process: 3 to 6 months recommended.

 

6. Recap of Life Cycle Stages 7:05

  • Initial contact starts at the Lead stage.

  • Qualification determines if the lead becomes an Opportunity.

  • Opportunity can eventually become a Customer.

 

7. Conclusion and Additional Notes 8:22

  • Ambassadors: Special customers who can serve as references.

  • Partners: Not relevant for the audience.

Leads are early-stage prospects who have shown some interest but are not yet qualified, while deals represent qualified leads that have serious potential for sales. I walk you through how leads are generated, such as when someone requests a price estimate, and how we can follow up with them to qualify or disqualify them. The goal is to move leads through different stages until we either convert them into deals or decide to let them go. Please take the time to review this process and consider how you can effectively manage your leads.
Article body:
Objective

This SOP outlines the steps for qualifying leads and creating deals in HubSpot to streamline the sales process.

Key Steps

 

Understanding Leads and Deals 0:00

  • Leads: Early stage sales prospects showing interest but not yet qualified.

  • Deals: Qualified leads that are serious potential customers with quantifiable sales potential.

 

Moving from Lead to Deal 0:29

  • Qualify the lead as a real opportunity.

  • Create a deal if the lead is qualified.

  • If disqualified, cease further action.

 

Generating Leads in HubSpot 1:14

  • Leads are generated when a potential customer interacts (e.g., estimating a price).

  • Example: Clicking a button in HubSpot generates a lead.

 

Following Up with Leads 1:44

  • Use the lead description to understand initial interest.

  • Follow up via email to start a conversation.

 

Qualifying Leads 2:00

  • Assess if the lead is a reattempt from previous outreach.

  • Move leads through different stages based on interaction.

 

Final Decision on Leads 2:32

  • After establishing contact, determine if the lead is qualified or disqualified.

  • Qualified leads move to deals; disqualified leads are marked as finished.

Cautionary Notes

  • Ensure to document all interactions with leads for future reference.

  • Avoid pursuing disqualified leads to save time and resources.

Tips for Efficiency

  • Use templates for follow-up emails to streamline communication.

  • Regularly review and update lead statuses to keep the pipeline organized.

In order to keep JSK rotary table in a good condition in the long run, the following adjustments and maintenances are inevitable:

•    Finding/Offsetting the zero position
•    Checking the worktable backlash
•    Setting backlash between Worm shaft and gear
•    Adjusting the zero-point guide block
•    Adjusting backlash between the worm gear and motor gear.

Finding/Offsetting the zero position

•    When the NC controller send a “Return to home” comment to the rotary table, the table homes in the clockwise direction as viewed from the platter/spindle.

•    When the micro-switch reaches the zero-point guide block (set at 1° ~ 3°), the rotary table starts to slow down and stabilizes at the mechanical home position. Measure the distance between the home position and real zero point by finding the variance in the horizontal direction via the height gauge. (Please see below diagram)

The height gauge

•    Enter the measured difference into the NC control for zero offset parameter.

Checking worktable backlash

The worktable backlash varies with temperature. When the temperature is 20℃, the minimum amount of backlash of worm gear ranges 10℃ to 15℃. The backlash decreases by 10℃ as the temperature increases by 10℃; vice versa, the backlash increases by 10℃ as the temperature decreases by 10℃.

•    Mount a dial indicator to the inside of the T-slot of the worktable.

•    First, insert a steel bar into another T-slot. Slowly push up the bar with a constant strength of 15~20 kilogram. Second, remove the bar and read the figure from the dial indicator. Third, insert the steel bar into the T-slot again, slowly push down the bar with the same strength, and read the other figure from the dial indicator. Forth, find the difference between the two figures which should be the worktable backlash

•    If the backlash amount is entered into the servo control as an adjusting parameter, the backlash can be adjusted to zero.

Setting backlash between Worm shaft and gear

An excessive amount of backlash between worm shaft and gear would lead to abnormal vibra-tion, resulting in increasing the cutting resistance. On the other hand, a very small amount of backlash would make the worm gear over-heated, or even get the worm gear stuck and further higher the value of electric current.
Thread of “dual lead worm” is designed from small to large pitch; the feature provides easy adjustment on the backlash between worm and worm gear. By shifting the worm longitudinal-ly, the highest indexing accuracy is maintained on worktable. Please see details of adjustment as follows:

Find the worm shaft cover on the lower side of side panel of rotary table

The M4 screw

Utilize the fastened M5 screws to take the cover away.

On the base of worm shaft assy, you can find six M7 screws used for fastening and six M5 stop-screws used for adjusting backlash.


The M7 screws
The M5 stop-screws

Equally loosen the M5 stop-screws

Equally fasten M7 screws in order to further push the base of worm shaft assy, accordingly causing some movement of the worktable.

Perform the above-mentioned “Checking worktable backlash” to check if the backlash stays within 0.01mm. If it doesn’t stay within 0.01mm, please repeat step 5), 6), and 7) until the ad-justed backlash fits.

Adjusting the zero-point guide block

Loosen 3/8 stop screw of oil drain plug, and then drain lubricant.

Find the round cover on the upper side of side panel of the rotary table

Loosen the M4 screw used to fasten the round cover

Utilize the fastened M5 screws to take the cover away. Then the zero-point guide block can be found in the hole

Loosen the M4 stop screw of the zero-point guide block

Adjust the zero-point guide block. The recommended range for adjustment is ± 5°.
After finalizing the adjustment, fasten the stop screw M4 of the zero-point guide block, and re-store the other parts.


Adjusting the backlash between worm and motor gear

Adjust the distance between worm and motor gear to address certain issues such as abnormal sound after installation, excessive current load due to a tight backlash…etc.


Loosen M8 stop screw of the adjusting hole in order to slightly enlarge the distance between worm and motor gear.

Loosen the motor-screws (which is used to fasten motor), and push the motor toward the back panel of rotary table. Then slightly tighten the motor-screws. By doing so, we can generate some spaces for adjusting the backlash.

Adjust the backlash by driving the M8 stop screw. Keep fine-tuning the screw until we find the best-balanced backlash which can minimize the current load and make less loud and sharp sounds while rotating.

Lubricating

In order to ensure the rotary table can perform well in the long term, the use of lubricant is inevitable. Please see the following points for attention:

  1. Lubricant can provide an appropriate oil film, preventing excessive friction, possible scoring, rust and oxidization. (The recommended viscosity grade: ISO VG 150)
  2. While lubricating, please ensure the lubricant will keep pure and can not get dirty. Any dirt, lint or foreign particle permeating the lubricant may damage the worm gear or other key components.
  3. Please fill lubricant until the Lubricant level surmounts the center line of oil window. This is the proper fill level.
  4. The lubricant change frequency actually depends on the usage rate. However, it’s recommended to completely change the lubricant every 6 months.

  2. While lubricating, please ensure the lubricant will keep pure and can not get dirty. Any dirt, lint or foreign particle permeating the lubricant may damage the worm gear or other key components.
  3. Please fill lubricant until the Lubricant level surmounts the center line of oil window. This is the proper fill level.
  4. The lubricant change frequency actually depends on the usage rate. However, it’s recommended to completely change the lubricant every 6 months.

In order to keep JSK rotary table in a good condition in the long run, the following adjustments and maintenances are inevitable:

•    Finding/Offsetting the zero position
•    Checking the worktable backlash
•    Setting backlash between Worm shaft and gear
•    Adjusting the zero-point guide block
•    Adjusting backlash between the worm gear and motor gear.

6.1 Finding/Offsetting the zero position


•    When the NC controller send a “Return to home” comment to the rotary table, the table homes in the clockwise direction as viewed from the platter/spindle.

•    When the micro-switch reaches the zero-point guide block (set at 1° ~ 3°), the rotary table starts to slow down and stabilizes at the mechanical home position. Measure the distance between the home position and real zero point by finding the variance in the horizontal direction via the height gauge. (Please see below diagram)

The height gauge

•    Enter the measured difference into the NC control for zero offset parameter.

6.2 Checking worktable backlash


The worktable backlash varies with temperature. When the temperature is 20℃, the minimum amount of backlash of worm gear ranges 10℃ to 15℃. The backlash decreases by 10℃ as the temperature increases by 10℃; vice versa, the backlash increases by 10℃ as the temperature decreases by 10℃.

1.    Mount a dial indicator to the inside of the T-slot of the worktable.

2.    First, insert a steel bar into another T-slot. Slowly push up the bar with a constant strength of 15~20 kilogram. Second, remove the bar and read the figure from the dial indicator. Third, insert the steel bar into the T-slot again, slowly push down the bar with the same strength, and read the other figure from the dial indicator. Forth, find the difference between the two figures which should be the worktable backlash

3.    If the backlash amount is entered into the servo control as an adjusting parameter, the backlash can be adjusted to zero.

6.3 Setting backlash between Worm shaft and gear


An excessive amount of backlash between worm shaft and gear would lead to abnormal vibration, resulting in increasing the cutting resistance. On the other hand, a very small amount of backlash would make the worm gear over-heated, or even get the worm gear stuck and further higher the value of electric current. Thread of “dual lead worm” is designed from small to large pitch; the feature provides easy adjustment on the backlash between worm and worm gear. By shifting the worm longitudinal-ly, the highest indexing accuracy is maintained on worktable. Please see details of adjustment as follows:

1. Find the worm shaft cover on the lower side of side panel of rotary table

2. Loosen the M4 screw used to fasten worm shaft cover

3. Utilize the fastened M5 screws to take the cover away.

4. On the base of worm shaft assy, you can find six M7 screws used for fastening and six M5 stop-screws used for adjusting backlash.

5. Equally loosen the M5 stop-screws

6. Equally fasten M7 screws in order to further push the base of worm shaft assy, accordingly causing some movement of the worktable.

7. Perform the above-mentioned “Checking worktable backlash” to check if the backlash stays within 0.01mm. If it doesn’t stay within 0.01mm, please repeat step 5), 6), and 7) until the ad-justed backlash fits.

6.4 Adjusting the zero-point guide block

1. Loosen 3/8 stop screw of oil drain plug, and then drain lubricant.

2. Find the round cover on the upper side of side panel of the rotary table

3. Loosen the M4 screw used to fasten the round cover

4. Utilize the fastened M5 screws to take the cover away. Then the zero-point guide block can be found in the hole

5. Loosen the M4 stop screw of the zero-point guide block

6. Adjust the zero-point guide block. The recommended range for adjustment is ± 5°.

7. After finalizing the adjustment, fasten the stop screw M4 of the zero-point guide block, and re-store the other parts.


6.5 Adjusting the backlash between worm and motor gear


Adjust the distance between worm and motor gear to address certain issues such as abnormal sound after installation, excessive current load due to a tight backlash…etc.

1. Loosen M8 stop screw of the adjusting hole in order to slightly enlarge the distance between worm and motor gear.

2. Loosen the motor-screws (which is used to fasten motor), and push the motor toward the back panel of rotary table. Then slightly tighten the motor-screws. By doing so, we can generate some spaces for adjusting the backlash.

3. Adjust the backlash by driving the M8 stop screw. Keep fine-tuning the screw until we find the best-balanced backlash which can minimize the current load and make less loud and sharp sounds while rotating.

1. Lubricating

In order to ensure the rotary table can perform well in the long term, the use of lubricant is inevitable. Please see the following points for attention:

  1. Lubricant can provide an appropriate oil film, preventing excessive friction, possible scoring, rust and oxidization. (The recommended viscosity grade: ISO VG 150)
  2. While lubricating, please ensure the lubricant will keep pure and can not get dirty. Any dirt, lint or foreign particle permeating the lubricant may damage the worm gear or other key components.
  3. Please fill lubricant until the Lubricant level surmounts the center line of oil window. This is the proper fill level.
  4. The lubricant change frequency actually depends on the usage rate. However, it’s recommended to completely change the lubricant every 6 months.

Motion Board and I/O Board Configuration

This section details the configuration parameters for the motion and I/O boards in SYNTEC CNC systems. ​

  • Motion board base address ranges from 512 to 65535, with an initial value of 800. ​
  • I/O board base address is set to 512. ​
  • The I/O board type can be selected from a range of 0 to 20, with an initial value of 7. ​
  • Various mappings for servo cards and their corresponding I/O base addresses are provided, including specific configurations for Servo4 and Servo6 cards. ​

Servo Board Type and Alarm Configuration

This section outlines the parameters for configuring servo board types and alarm settings.

  • Servo board type ranges from 0 to 9, with an initial value of 3. ​
  • Alarm types for Servo6 can be set to Normal Open or Normal Close, with an initial value of 0. ​
  • The clock source for the servo board can be set to three options, with an initial value of 2.

Control Precision and Error Tolerance Settings

This section describes parameters related to control precision and error tolerance in the CNC system.

  • Control precision can be set between 1 and 3, affecting the basic length unit (BLU) and least input unit (LIU). ​
  • HSHP chord error tolerance ranges from 1 to 100, with an initial value of 15, determining the maximum permissible tolerance for block path approaches.

Axis Configuration and Feedback Parameters

This section covers the configuration of axes, including motor command polarity and encoder resolution.

  • Motor command polarity for axes can be set to 0 (same direction) or 1 (reverse direction). ​
  • Encoder resolution ranges from 10 to 2,500,000 pulses, with a default of 1250. ​
  • Dual feedback settings for axes include feedback type and resolution, with specific parameters for each axis. ​

Gain and Control Loop Settings

This section details the gain settings for motor velocity and position control loops. ​

  • Gain of the motor velocity loop ranges from 1 to 8000 RPM/V, with an initial value of 200. ​
  • Loop gain for the position loop can be set between 1 and 3000, with an initial value of 30. ​
  • Gear numbers for ballscrew and motor sides can be set from 1 to 999,999,999, with an initial value of 1. ​

Cutting and Acceleration Parameters

This section outlines parameters related to cutting acceleration and feed rates. ​

  • Maximum cutting feedrate is set between 6 and 3,600,000 mm/min, with an initial value of 5000. ​
  • Cutting acceleration time can be set from 0 to 60,000 ms, with an initial value of 300 ms. ​
  • Post cutting bell-shaped acceleration time is adjustable, with an initial value of 20 ms. ​

Tool Compensation and Travel Settings

This section describes settings for tool length compensation and rapid travel modes. ​

  • Tool length compensation restoration mode can be set to restore or not restore, with an initial value of 0 (unrestore). ​
  • Rapid travel mode can be set to linear or independent, with an initial value of 0 (linear).

Reserve Local Coordinate and Workpiece System

This section outlines parameters for reserving local coordinates and workpiece coordinate systems after reset. ​

  • Pr413: Reserve local coordinate G92 (G92.1) after reset with options 0 (not reserve), 1 (reserve after reset), and 2 (not reserve after reset or restart). ​
  • Pr414: Reserve workpiece coordinate system after reset with options 0 (default to G54), 1 (do not reserve), and 2 (no reserve after reset or power off). ​

Tool Length and Rigid Tapping Parameters

This section details parameters related to tool length reservation and rigid tapping settings.

  • Pr415: Reserve current tool length after reset or power off with options 0 (not reserve) and 1 (reserve). ​
  • Pr416: Rigid tapping coupling time set between 0 to 6000 ms. ​
  • Pr417: Rigid tapping velocity gain ranges from 0 to 200, affecting Z-axis following spindle. ​
  • Pr418: Rigid tapping acceleration/deceleration gain ranges from 0 to 200, impacting Z-axis acceleration. ​
  • Pr419: Rigid tapping spindle deceleration time set between 0 to 6000 ms. ​

Axis Cutting and Rapid Travel Parameters

This section describes parameters for axis cutting in-position windows and rapid travel settings.

  • Pr421~440: Axis cutting in-position window set between 0 to 300000 BLU, with a default of 30. ​
  • Pr441~460: Axis rapid travel (G00) acceleration time set between 0 to 60000 ms, with a default of 200 ms. ​
  • Pr461~480: Axis max. rapid travel (G00) feedrate ranges from 6 to 360000 mm/min, with a default of 10000 mm/min. ​
  • Pr481~500: Rapid travel in-position window set between 0 to 300000 BLU, with a default of 30. ​

Backlash Compensation and Error Parameters

This section covers backlash compensation settings and error checks for axes.

  • Pr1221~1240: Backlash compensation start options include 0 (OFF), 1 (Linear Guideway ON), and 2 (Box Guideway ON). ​
  • Pr1241~1260: G00 and G01 backlash compensation values range from -999999 to 999999 BLU, with defaults of 0. ​
  • Pr1281~1300: Backlash critical speed set between 0 to 3000 mm/min, with a default of 0. ​
  • Pr1301~1320: Pitch error compensation type options include 0 (no compensation), 1 (unidirectional), and 2 (bidirectional).

Spindle and Tool Parameters

This section outlines parameters related to spindle settings and tool management.

  • Pr1791: Spindle motor type options include 0 (frequency motor) to 4 (Syntec spindle), with a default of 0. ​
  • Pr1801~1810: Spindle maximum speed ranges from 0 to 80000 RPM, with a default of 10000 RPM. ​
  • Pr3215: Call program mode when selecting the tool options include 0 (T Code will not call T0000) to 2 (call T0000 as MACRO). ​
  • Pr3228: Enable tool manager options include 0 (disable) and 1 (enable).

System and Control Parameters

This section describes various system settings and control parameters.

  • Pr3202: I/O scan time set between 100 to 5000 ms, with a default of 3000 ms. ​
  • Pr3203: Interpolation time interval set between 500 to 200000 ms, with a default of 2000 ms. ​
  • Pr3221: Debug level options include 0 (disable) to 2 (single-step block of macro).
  • Pr3802: Default feedrate control mode options include 0 (G64) and 1 (G62).

Paralleled Executing Multiple M Code

This parameter allows for the simultaneous execution of multiple M codes in a single block. ​

  • Parameter No: 3810
  • Range: [0~1], with 0 being Off and 1 being On.
  • Initial value is 0, and it requires a restart to apply changes.

Start Address of Persistent Working Variables

This setting determines the starting address for global variables that retain their values after power off. ​

  • Parameter No: 3811
  • Range: [0~400], where 0 resets all data after power off. ​
  • Setting an address (e.g., 100) allows data from @100 to @400 to persist after power off. ​
  • Initial value is 0, and it requires a restart to apply changes.

Number of Extended Global Variables

This parameter sets the total number of extended global variables available for use. ​

  • Parameter No: 3813
  • Range: [0~20000], with an initial value of 0.
  • Setting 1000 allows for variables from @60000 to @60999.
  • Requires a restart to apply changes.

Tool Radius Compensation Mode

This setting defines how tool radius compensation is applied during machining. ​

  • Parameter No: 3815
  • Range: [0~2], with 0 for normal mode, 1 for preview mode, and 2 for a different normal mode.
  • Initial value is 0, and it requires a reset to apply changes.

Tool Length Compensation Mode

This parameter specifies the mode for tool length compensation during machining. ​

  • Parameter No: 3816
  • Range: [0~2], where 0 is for Z-axis only, 1 is for a single axis perpendicular to the cutting plane, and 2 is for multiple axes.
  • Initial value is 0, and it requires a reset to apply changes.

Fatal Dual Feedback Error

This parameter sets the maximum allowed error between motor encoder and ruler feedback signals.

  • Parameter No: 3817
  • Range: [0~100000], with a default value of 10000.
  • Setting to 0 disables the checking function. ​
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

Dual Feedback Self-Detect Error

This parameter monitors the difference in pulse counts between two indexes for dual feedback systems.

  • Parameter No: 3818
  • Range: [0~50], with a default value of 0.
  • If set to 0, the self-checking function is disabled. ​
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

Overcut Check Mode

This setting determines how the system checks for overcutting during machining.

  • Parameter No: 3819
  • Range: [0~2], where 0 means no check, 1 checks and alarms if overcut, and 2 checks and fits the path without alarming. ​
  • Initial value is 0, and it requires a reset to apply changes.

Minimal Deceleration Ratio for Inner Circular Cutting

This parameter restricts the minimum deceleration ratio during inner circular cutting operations. ​

  • Parameter No: 3820
  • Range: [1~100]%, with an initial value of 2%.
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

Coupling Master and Slave Axis Settings

These parameters define the master and slave axes for coupling operations. ​

  • Parameter Nos: 3821 (master axis) and 3822 (slave axis). ​
  • Range: [0~20], with initial values of 0.
  • Requires a restart to apply changes.

Coupling Ratio Factor for Master and Slave Axes

These parameters set the movement ratio for coupled axes.

  • Parameter Nos: 3823 (master ratio) and 3824 (slave ratio).
  • Range: [1~999999], with initial values of 0.
  • Requires a restart to apply changes.

Coupling Type for Master and Slave Axes

This parameter defines the type of coupling between master and slave axes. ​

  • Parameter No: 3825
  • Range: [0~5], with 0 to cancel coupling and 1 to 5 for different coupling types. ​
  • Initial value is 0, and it requires a restart to apply changes.

Coupling Time Settings

These parameters set the time for coupling and decoupling actions.

  • Parameter Nos: 3826 (couple time) and 3827 (decouple time).
  • Range: [0~60000] ms, with no initial values specified.
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

Discharge Resolution and Ignition Delay

These parameters define the resolution and ignition delay for discharge operations.

  • Parameter Nos: 3831 (resolution) and 3832 (ignition delay).
  • Range for resolution: [1~999999999] ns, initial value 1000.
  • Range for ignition delay: [0~999999999] ns, initial value 0. ​
  • Requires a restart to apply changes.

Initial Command Mode Settings

This parameter sets the default command mode for the system.

  • Parameter No: 3837
  • Range: [0~2], with 0 as default (G90).
  • Requires a restart to apply changes.

Measurement of Tool Contact Surface Position

These parameters measure the contact surface positions for tool setup. ​

  • Parameter Nos: 3841 to 3844 for Z+ and Z-, X+, and X- positions.
  • Range: [-999999999~999999999] BLU, with initial values of 0.
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

Tool Break Handle Program Number

This parameter sets the program number for handling tool breaks. ​

  • Parameter No: 3851
  • Range: [0~999999], with 0 indicating no tool break handling. ​
  • Initial value is 0, and it requires a reset to apply changes.

Enable Halted Point Return

This parameter allows for returning to a halted point in the program. ​

  • Parameter No: 3852
  • Range: [0~1], with 1 enabling the return function.
  • Initial value is 0, and it requires a reset to apply changes.

2nd to 4th Axis Coupling Settings

These parameters define coupling settings for additional axes. ​

  • Parameter Nos: 3861 to 3890 for 2nd to 4th axes. ​
  • Requires a restart to apply changes.

DC Protocol Role Settings

This parameter defines the role of the DC protocol in communication. ​

  • Parameter No: 3901
  • Range: [0~1], with 0 for controller and 1 for PC and device.
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

File Transfer and Macro Program Port Numbers

These parameters set the port numbers for file transfer and macro programs. ​

  • Parameter Nos: 3903 (file transfer) and 3905 (macro program). ​
  • Range: [1~2], with initial values of 1 for file transfer and 2 for macro.
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

COM1 Communication Settings

These parameters define the communication settings for COM1.

  • Parameter Nos: 3921 to 3929 for baud rate, data bits, exchange code type, etc. ​
  • Various ranges and initial values specified, requiring a reset to apply changes.

Chopping Axis Settings

These parameters define settings for the chopping axis.

  • Parameter Nos: 3951 to 3956 for ID, reference position, dead positions, feedrate, and compensation factor.
  • Various ranges and initial values specified, requiring a reset to apply changes.

COM3 Communication Settings

These parameters define the communication settings for COM3.

  • Parameter Nos: 3961 to 3970, similar to COM1 settings. ​
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

Default Cutting Feedrate Settings

This parameter sets the default cutting feedrate for machining operations. ​

  • Parameter No: 4070
  • Range: [6~3600000], with an initial value of 1000.
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

Straightness Offset Moving Axis Position

These parameters define the positions for straightness compensation.

  • Parameter Nos: 7001 to 7025 for offset positions.
  • Range: [0~100], with an initial value of 0.
  • Requires a restart to apply changes.

Pitch Error Compensation Table

This parameter sets the compensation values for pitch errors. ​

  • Parameter Nos: 8001 to 10000 for compensation values.
  • Range: [-999999~999999], with an initial value of 0.
  • Requires a reset to apply changes.

Lathe-Specific Parameters Overview

This section outlines parameters specific to lathe operations, including drilling, tapping, threading, and more.

  • Various parameters (4001 to 4047) with specific ranges and initial values.
  • Each parameter serves a unique function related to lathe operations.
  • Requires resets to apply changes as specified.
